genesis.1:1-2: The first verse is a summary heading for the whole account. Verse 2 then describes the earth as unformed and unfilled, the two problems the six days address in turn: days 1–3 give form, days 4–6 fill it.
genesis.1:3-5: God creates by speaking. Light comes before the sun of day 4, which keeps the focus on God as the source of light rather than any created body.

john.1:1-5: John opens with the same words as Genesis 1:1, “In the beginning,” and places the Word there before anything was made. Three statements build on each other: the Word already existed, the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Creation, life and light are then traced back to Him, which prepares the reader for the light-and-darkness theme that runs through the whole Gospel.
john.1:6-8: John the Baptist is introduced as a witness, not as the Light. The repetition is deliberate: his role is to point away from himself (compare John 3:30).
john.1:9-13: The rejection of verses 10–11 is set against the welcome of verse 12. Becoming “children of God” is described as a birth whose source is God, not human descent or decision.
john.1:14: The word rendered “made His dwelling” is the verb form of the Greek word for tent or tabernacle. The language recalls God’s presence among Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 40:34) and the glory that filled it.
john.1:15-18: Grace and truth are contrasted with the law given through Moses, not as opposites but as fulfilment. Verse 18 closes the prologue where it began: the one who is with the Father is the one who makes Him known.

psalms.23:1-3: David speaks of the LORD as a shepherd who provides rest, water, restoration and guidance, all “for the sake of His name.” The care given rests on God’s own character.
psalms.23:4-6: At verse 4 the psalm turns from speaking about God to speaking to Him: “You are with me.” The image then changes from shepherd to host, who sets a table and anoints the guest.
